analysis.one_liner: Bans federal officials and their families from issuing, sponsoring, or endorsing cryptocurrencies, meme coins, and stablecoins while in office.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced June 23, 2025 with 10 Senate Democratic cosponsors, was sent to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee and has had no hearing, markup, or floor vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for federal officials and their immediate family members to issue, sponsor, or endorse crypto assets — including cryptocurrencies, meme coins, non-fungible tokens, and payment stablecoins — while serving, for 180 days before taking office, and for two years after leaving. Violators would face civil fines, repayment of any profits, and in serious cases prison terms of up to 5 to 15 years. It would also require officials to disclose any digital-asset holdings over $1,000 and require approved stablecoin issuers to certify, on a public database, that no official profits from their coins.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who buy crypto assets: the bill targets the practice of officials putting their names on coins sold to the public, which can push retail investors into assets that often lose most of their value. Taxpayers also gain from the conflict-of-interest rules, and the public gains visibility into officials' digital-asset holdings.

how_it_helps.text: Bars covered officials and their immediate family members from issuing, sponsoring, or endorsing digital assets — including meme coins, tokens, NFTs, and payment stablecoins — during their term, for 180 days before it, and for two years after [S2].
Attaches real teeth: civil penalties of up to $25,000 per violation, 10% of the interest's value, or the amount of gain, plus disgorgement of profits to the Treasury [S2].
Creates criminal penalties — up to 5 years for profiting from a violation that costs others $1 million or more, and up to 15 years where the violation involves bribery or insider trading [S2].
Requires officials to disclose cryptocurrencies, meme coins, tokens, NFTs, and stablecoins held over $1,000 on their annual financial reports [S2].
Requires approved stablecoin issuers to certify quarterly that no public official profits from their coins, with the certifications posted publicly and approval revoked if they fail to file [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent officials and their families lose the ability to launch or promote digital assets for money, and crypto issuers lose the marketing value of an official's name and likeness. Compliance costs fall on stablecoin issuers, who must file certifications to keep their approval.
analysis.who_pays_short: Officials, their families, and crypto issuers

drawbacks.text: The bill covers only digital assets — it does nothing about officials trading individual stocks or other securities, which is the conflict-of-interest concern most ethics legislation has targeted [S2].
Enforcement runs through the Attorney General, a politically appointed official, so a president's Justice Department would decide whether to sue members of that same administration or party [S2].

The ban leaves a large carve-out: officials may still buy, sell, and hold digital assets that are 'routinely accessible to any member of the public,' so it stops official coin launches and endorsements but not officials' own crypto trading [S2].

An honest supporter would concede that civil penalties capped at $25,000 or 10% of value can be small next to what a successful meme coin raises, and the stablecoin-issuer certification scheme asks private companies to police officials' interests, an unusual division of labor [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would close a specific, real loophole — officials cashing in on coins sold to their own supporters — with meaningful civil and criminal penalties. But it is deliberately narrow: it touches only crypto, leaves routine officials' trading of other assets untouched, and relies on an appointed Attorney General to enforce it. It is a targeted fix, not a comprehensive conflict-of-interest law.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Sen. Adam Schiff introduced the bill on June 23, 2025, joined by 10 Democratic senators as cosponsors [S2][S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, and no further action of any kind after the referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent officials and their families keep the option to profit from digital-asset ventures, and crypto issuers keep the ability to use officials' names and likenesses to sell coins, since the restriction never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 10 cosponsors are Senate Democrats; no Republican has cosponsored, and the bill has sat in a committee chaired by a Republican without action.

industries.industry: Public officials and their immediate families
industries.note: The bill would end their ability to issue, sponsor, or endorse coins sold to the public, and to profit from them, with disgorgement of profits and prison exposure for serious violations. Officials' gains from promoted coins come largely at the expense of retail buyers.

Issuers lose one of the most valuable marketing tools in the sector — an official's name on a coin — since the bill defines 'endorsement' to include use of an official's name and likeness, even in a coin's title.

Approved issuers would face a new quarterly certification duty and risk having their approval revoked if they fail to file, adding compliance cost, but the public database of certifications could also raise confidence in the sector.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has sat in committee since its June 2025 referral with no hearing, markup, or vote. Ethics measures that restrict officeholders' own finances rarely reach the floor without bipartisan leadership backing, and no Senate Republican has cosponsored this one, so the most likely path is that it remains in committee and expires when this Congress ends in January 2027, unless the committee schedules it or a broader ethics bill absorbs its provisions.
